{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
{{main|Perturbation theory}}
In mathematics, an '''eigenvalue perturbation''' problem is that of finding the [[eigenvector|eigenvectors and eigenvalues]] of a system <math> Ax=\lambda x </math> that is [[perturbation theory|perturbed]] from one with known eigenvectors and eigenvalues <math> A_0 x_0=\lambda_0x_0 </math>. This is useful for studying how sensitive the original system's eigenvectors and eigenvalues <math> x_{0i}, \lambda_{0i}, i=1, \dots n </math>  are to changes in the system. 
This type of analysis was popularized by [[John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh|Lord Rayleigh]], in his investigation of harmonic vibrations of a string perturbed by small inhomogeneities.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rayleigh |first=J. W. S. |url=https://archive.org/details/ost-physics-the_theory_of_sound |title=The theory of Sound |publisher=Macmillan |year=1894 |isbn=1-152-06023-6 |edition=2nd |volume=1 |location=London |pages=114–118}}</ref>

The derivations in this article are essentially self-contained and can be found in many texts on [[numerical linear algebra]] or numerical [[functional analysis]].
This article is focused on the case of the perturbation of a simple eigenvalue, as opposed to a 
[[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors#Algebraic multiplicity|multiplicity of eigenvalues]].

== Motivation for generalized eigenvalues ==
Many scientific fields use [[eigenvalues]] to obtain solutions. [[Eigendecomposition of a matrix#Generalized eigenspaces|Generalized eigenvalue problems]] are less widespread but are key in the study of [[vibrations]]. They are useful when the [[Galerkin method|Galerkin]] or [[Rayleigh–Ritz method|Rayleigh-Ritz]] methods are used to find approximate solutions of partial differential equations modeling vibrations of structures such as strings and plates - Courant (1943) 
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Courant|first1= R. |title=Variational Methods for the Solution of Problems of Equilibrium and Vibrations.  |date=1943| journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society| volume=49| pages=1–23| doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1943-07818-4 |doi-access=free|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society/volume-49/issue-1/Variational-methods-for-the-solution-of-problems-of-equilibrium-and/bams/1183504922.pdf}}</ref> is fundamental. The [[finite element method]] is  a widespread particular case.

In [[classical mechanics]], generalized eigenvalues may crop up when inspecting vibrations of [[Vibration#Multiple degrees of freedom systems and mode shapes|multiple degrees of freedom]] systems close to equilibrium. In this case the [[kinetic energy]] provides the [[mass matrix]] <math> M </math>, the potential strain energy provides the rigidity matrix <math> K </math>.<ref>
{{ cite journal 
| last1= Weinstein 
| first1=A. 
| date=1941
| title=Les vibrations et le calcul des variations.
|issue=2 
| pages=36–55 
|journal=Portugaliae Mathematica 
| volume=2 
| url=http://eudml.org/doc/114572 
|language=French }}
</ref>

With both methods, the following system of differential equations or [[matrix differential equation]] is derived:
<math> M \ddot x+B \dot x +Kx=0 </math> with the mass matrix <math> M </math> , the [[damping matrix]] <math> B </math> and the rigidity matrix <math> K </math>. If the damping effect is neglected, <math> B=0</math>, and a solution of the form <math> x=e^{i \omega t} u</math> is assumed,<math>u </math> and <math>\omega^2 </math>are obtained as solutions to the generalized eigenvalue problem <math> -\omega^2 M u+Ku =0 </math>.

==Setting of perturbation for a generalized eigenvalue problem==
Suppose the solutions to the [[generalized eigenvalue problem]] are known to be

:<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad (0)</math>

where <math>\mathbf{K}_0</math> and <math>\mathbf{M}_0</math> are matrices. That is, we know the eigenvalues {{math|''λ''<sub>0''i''</sub>}} and eigenvectors {{math|'''x'''<sub>0''i''</sub>}} for {{math|''i'' {{=}} 1, ..., ''N''}}. An important note is that the eigenvalues are required to be distinct.

In order to perturb the matrices, one must find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of
:<math>\mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i \qquad (1)</math>
where
:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K} &= \mathbf{K}_0 + \delta \mathbf{K}\\
\mathbf{M} &= \mathbf{M}_0 + \delta \mathbf{M}
\end{align}</math>

with the perturbations <math>\delta\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\delta\mathbf{M}</math> much smaller than <math>\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\mathbf{M}</math> respectively. Then the new eigenvalues and eigenvectors are expected to be similar to the original, plus small perturbations:

:<math>\begin{align}
\lambda_i &= \lambda_{0i}+\delta\lambda_{i} \\
\mathbf{x}_i &= \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\mathbf{x}_{i} 
\end{align}</math>

==Steps==
Under the assumption that the matrices are [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]], [[positive-definite matrix|positive definite]], and assume the eigenvectors are scaled such that

: <math>\mathbf{x}_{0j}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} = \delta_{ij}, \quad 
</math><math>\mathbf{x}_{i}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{j}= \delta_{ij} \qquad(2)
 
</math>

where {{math|''δ<sub>ij</sub>''}} is the [[Kronecker delta]]. 
Now the equation to be solved is

:<math>\mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}_i - \lambda_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i=0. </math>
In this article, the study is restricted to first order perturbation.

===First order expansion of the equation ===
Substituting in (1) results in

:<math>(\mathbf{K}_0+\delta \mathbf{K})(\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta \mathbf{x}_{i}) = \left (\lambda_{0i}+\delta\lambda_{i} \right ) \left (\mathbf{M}_0+ \delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \left (\mathbf{x}_{0i}+\delta\mathbf{x}_{i} \right ),</math>

which expands to

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} &+ \delta \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{K}_0\delta \mathbf{x}_i + \delta \mathbf{K}\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \\[6pt]
&\lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}+\lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +\delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \\
& \quad \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i.
\end{align}</math>

Canceling from (0) (<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}</math>) leaves

:<math>\begin{align}
\delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + & \mathbf{K}_0\delta \mathbf{x}_i + \delta \mathbf{K}\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \\ & \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i +  \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i.
\end{align}</math>

Removing the higher-order terms, this simplifies to

:<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad(3)</math>
:In other words, <math>\delta \lambda_i</math>  no longer denotes the exact variation of the eigenvalue but its first order approximation.

As the matrix is symmetric, the unperturbed eigenvectors are <math> M </math> orthogonal and so can be used as a basis for the perturbed eigenvectors. 
This is the same as

:<math>\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} \qquad (4) \quad </math> with <math> \varepsilon_{ij}=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T M \delta \mathbf{x}_i </math>,
where {{math|''ε<sub>ij</sub>''}} are small constants that are to be determined.

In the same way, substituting in (2), and removing higher order terms, <math>\delta\mathbf{x}_j \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0j} \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_{i} 
+  \mathbf{x}_{0j} \delta \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}=0 \quad{(5)}</math>

The derivation is then split into two paths.

==== First path: get first eigenvalue perturbation ====
=====  Eigenvalue perturbation =====
:Starting with (3)<math>\quad \mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}; </math>which is then left multiplied with <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T </math> along with using (2) as well as its first order variation (5); one gets

:<math> \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i
</math>
or
:<math> \delta \lambda_i=\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} -\lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}
</math>
This is the first order perturbation of the generalized [[Rayleigh quotient]]  with fixed <math>x_{0i}</math>: <math> R(K,M;x_{0i})=x_{0i}^T K x_{0i}/x_{0i}^TMx_{0i}, \text{ with }x_{0i}^TMx_{0i}=1 </math>

Moreover, for <math>M=I</math>, the formula <math>\delta \lambda_i = x_{0i} ^T \delta K x_{0i}</math> should be compared with [[Bauer–Fike theorem|Bauer-Fike]] theorem which provides a bound for eigenvalue perturbation.

===== Eigenvector perturbation =====
One then left multiplies (3) with <math> x_{0j}^T </math> for <math> j \neq i </math> and get
:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}. </math>
Recalling that <math> \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T K=\lambda_{0j} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^TM \text{ and } \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}=0,
</math> for <math> j \neq i </math>, one may substitute for

:<math>\lambda_{0j} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} . </math>
or
:<math>(\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i}) \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} =  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}  . </math>
As the eigenvalues are assumed to be simple, for <math> j \neq i </math>
:<math> \epsilon_{ij}=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i =\frac{-\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}}{ (\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i})} ,  i=1, \dots N; j=1, \dots N; j \neq i. </math>
Moreover (5) (the first order variation of (2) ) yields
<math> 2 \epsilon_{ii}=2 \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta x_i=-\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta M \mathbf{x}_{0i} .</math>
All of the components of <math> \delta x_i </math> have now been obtained.

==== Second path: Straightforward manipulations ====
Substituting (4) into (3) and rearranging gives
:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} && (5) \\
\sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} && \\ (\text{applying } \mathbf{K}_0 \text{ to the sum} )\\
\sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \lambda_{0j} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} && (\text{using Eq. } (1) )
\end{align}</math>

Because the eigenvectors are {{math|'''M'''<sub>0</sub>}}-orthogonal when {{math|'''M'''<sub>0</sub>}} is positive definite, one can remove the summations by left-multiplying by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top</math>:

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \varepsilon_{ii} \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. </math>

By use of equation (1) again:

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{K}_0 \varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad (6) </math>

The two terms containing {{math|''ε<sub>ii</sub>''}} are equal because left-multiplying (1) by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top</math> gives

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top\mathbf{K}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Canceling those terms in (6) leaves

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Rearranging gives

:<math>\delta\lambda_i  = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K}- \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top\mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}}</math>

But by (2), this denominator is equal to 1. Thus

:<math>\delta\lambda_i  = \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Then, as <math>\lambda_i \neq \lambda_k </math> for <math>i \neq k</math>  (this is the assumption of simple eigenvalues) by left-multiplying equation (5) by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0k}^\top</math>:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ik} = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0k} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0k}}, \qquad i\neq k.</math>

Or by changing the name of the indices:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0j} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}}, \qquad i\neq j.</math>

To find {{math|''ε<sub>ii</sub>''}}, using the fact that

:<math>\mathbf{x}^\top_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i = 1</math>

implies:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ii}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

== Summary of the first order perturbation result ==
In the case where '''''all the matrices are Hermitian positive definite and all the eigenvalues are distinct''''', 
:<math>\begin{align}
\lambda_i &= \lambda_{0i} + \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i} \\ 
\mathbf{x}_i &= \mathbf{x}_{0i} \left (1 - \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} \right ) + \sum_{j=1\atop j\neq i}^N \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0j}\left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}} \mathbf{x}_{0j}
\end{align}</math>

for infinitesimal <math>\delta\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\delta\mathbf{M}</math> (the higher order terms in (3) being neglected).

A proof that higher order terms may be neglect may be derived using the implicit function theorem.

== Theoretical derivation ==

=== Perturbation of an implicit function. ===
In the next paragraph, we shall  use the [[Implicit function theorem]] (Statement of the theorem ); we  notice that for a continuously differentiable function <math>f:\R^{n+m} \to \R^m, \; f: (x,y) \mapsto f(x,y)</math>, with an invertible Jacobian matrix  <math> J_{f,b}(x_0,y_0) </math>,  from a point <math> (x_0,y_0) </math> solution of  <math>f(x_0,y_0)=0 </math>, we get solutions of <math>f(x,y)=0 </math> with <math> x</math> close to <math> x_0</math> in the form <math> y=g(x)</math> where <math> g</math> is a continuously [[differentiable function]] ; moreover the Jacobian marix of <math> g </math> is provided by the linear system  
 <math> J_{f,y}(x,g(x)) J_{g,x}(x)+J_{f,x}(x,g(x))=0  \quad (6) </math>.
As soon as the hypothesis of the theorem is satisfied, the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian matrix]] of <math> g </math> may be computed with a first order  expansion of
<math> f(x_0+ \delta x, y_0+\delta y)=0 </math>, we get

<math> J_{f,x}(x,g(x)) \delta x+ J_{f,y}(x,g(x))\delta y=0 </math>; as <math>\delta y=J_{g,x}(x) \delta x </math>, it is equivalent to equation <math> (6) </math>.

=== Eigenvalue perturbation: a theoretical basis. ===
We use the previous paragraph (Perturbation of an implicit function) with somewhat different notations suited to eigenvalue perturbation; we introduce <math> \tilde{f}:  \R^{2n^2}  \times \R^{n+1} \to \R^{n+1}</math>, with
*<math> \tilde{f} (K,M, \lambda,x)= \binom{f(K,M,\lambda,x)}{f_{n+1}(x)}</math> with 
<math>f(K,M, \lambda,x) =Kx -\lambda x, f_{n+1}(M,x)=x^T Mx -1</math>. In order to use the [[Implicit function theorem]], we study the invertibility of the Jacobian <math> J_{\tilde{f};\lambda,x} (K,M;\lambda_{0i},x_{0i})</math> with

<math> J_{\tilde{f};\lambda,x} (K,M;\lambda_i,x_i)(\delta \lambda,\delta x)=\binom{-Mx_i}{0} \delta \lambda  +\binom{K-\lambda M}{2 x_i^T M} \delta x_i</math>. Indeed, the solution of

<math>J_{\tilde{f};\lambda_{0i},x_{0i} } (K,M;\lambda_{0i},x_{0i})(\delta \lambda_i,\delta x_i)=</math><math>\binom{y}{y_{n+1}} </math> may be derived with computations similar to the derivation of the expansion.

<math display="block">  \delta \lambda_i= -x_{0i}^T y, \; \text{ and } (\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j})x_{0j}^T M \delta x_i=x_j^T y, j=1, \dots, n, j \neq i\;;
</math> <math>
 \text{ or }x_{0j}^T M \delta x_i=x_j^T y/(\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}), \text{ and }
\; 2x_{0i}^TM \delta x_i=y_{n+1} </math>

When <math> \lambda_i</math> is a simple eigenvalue, as the eigenvectors <math>x_{0j}, j=1, \dots,n </math> form an orthonormal  basis, for any right-hand side, we have obtained one solution therefore,  the Jacobian is invertible.

The [[Implicit function theorem#Statement of the theorem|implicit function theorem]] provides a continuously differentiable function 
<math> (K,M) \mapsto (\lambda_i(K,M), x_i(K,M))</math>
hence the expansion with [[Big O notation#Little-o notation|little o notation]]:
<math> \lambda_i=\lambda_{0i}+ \delta \lambda_i +o(\| \delta K \|+\|\delta M \|)</math>
<math> x_i=x_{0i}+ \delta x_i +o(\| \delta K \|+\|\delta M \|)</math>.
with

<math> \delta \lambda_i=\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} -\lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i};</math> <math> \delta x_i=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_{0j} 
\text{ with}
</math><math>  \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i =\frac{-\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}}{ (\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i})} ,  i=1, \dots n; j=1, \dots n; j \neq i.</math>
This is the first order expansion of the perturbed eigenvalues and eigenvectors. which is proved.

==Results of sensitivity analysis with respect to the entries of the matrices==
===The results ===
This means it is possible to efficiently do a [[sensitivity analysis]] on {{math|''λ<sub>i</sub>''}} as a function of changes in the entries of the matrices. (Recall that the matrices are symmetric and so changing {{math|'''K'''<sub>''k''ℓ</sub>}} will also change {{math|'''K'''<sub>ℓ''k''</sub>}}, hence the {{math|(2 − ''δ''<sub>''k''ℓ</sub>)}} term

== Why generalized eigenvalues? ==
In the entry [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|applications of eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] we find numerous scientific fields in which eigenvalues are used to obtain solutions.  [[Eigendecomposition of a matrix#Generalized eigenspaces|Generalized eigenvalue problems]] are less widespread but are a key in the study of [[vibrations]].
They are useful when we use the  [[Galerkin method]]  or  [[Rayleigh–Ritz method|Rayleigh-Ritz method]] to find approximate 
solutions of partial differential equations modeling vibrations of structures such as strings and plates;  the paper of Courant (1943) 
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Courant|first1= R. |title=Variational Methods for the Solution of Problems of Equilibrium and Vibrations.  |date=1943| journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society| volume=49| pages=1–23| doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1943-07818-4 |doi-access=free|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society/volume-49/issue-1/Variational-methods-for-the-solution-of-problems-of-equilibrium-and/bams/1183504922.pdf}}</ref> is fundamental.  The [[Finite element method]] is  a widespread particular case.

In classical mechanics, generalized eigenvalues may crop up when we look for vibrations of  [[Vibration#Multiple degrees of freedom systems and mode shapes|multiple degrees of freedom]] systems close to equilibrium; the kinetic energy provides the mass matrix <math> M </math>, the potential strain energy provides the rigidity matrix <math> K </math>.
For further details, see the first section of this article of Weinstein (1941, in French)
<ref>
{{ cite journal 
| last1= Weinstein 
| first1=A. 
| date=1941
| title=Les vibrations et le calcul des variations.
|issue=2 
| pages=36–55 
|journal=Portugaliae Mathematica 
| volume=2 
| url=http://eudml.org/doc/114572 
|language=French }}
</ref>

With both methods, we obtain a system of differential equations or [[Matrix differential equation]]
<math> M \ddot x+B \dot x +Kx=0 </math> with the mass matrix <math> M </math> , the damping matrix <math> B </math> and the rigidity matrix <math> K </math>. If we neglect the damping effect, we use <math> B=0</math>, we can look for a solution  of the following form <math> x=e^{i \omega t} u</math>; we obtain that <math>u </math> and <math>\omega^2 </math>are solution of the generalized eigenvalue problem <math> -\omega^2 M u+Ku =0 </math>

==Setting of perturbation for a generalized eigenvalue problem==
Suppose we have solutions to the [[generalized eigenvalue problem]],

:<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad (0)</math>

where <math>\mathbf{K}_0</math> and <math>\mathbf{M}_0</math> are matrices. That is, we know the eigenvalues {{math|''λ''<sub>0''i''</sub>}} and eigenvectors {{math|'''x'''<sub>0''i''</sub>}} for {{math|''i'' {{=}} 1, ..., ''N''}}. It is also required that '''''the eigenvalues are distinct'''.''

Now suppose we want to change the matrices by a small amount. That is, we want to find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of
:<math>\mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i \qquad (1)</math>
where
:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K} &= \mathbf{K}_0 + \delta \mathbf{K}\\
\mathbf{M} &= \mathbf{M}_0 + \delta \mathbf{M}
\end{align}</math>

with the perturbations <math>\delta\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\delta\mathbf{M}</math> much smaller than <math>\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\mathbf{M}</math> respectively. Then we expect the new eigenvalues and eigenvectors to be similar to the original, plus small perturbations:

:<math>\begin{align}
\lambda_i &= \lambda_{0i}+\delta\lambda_{i} \\
\mathbf{x}_i &= \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\mathbf{x}_{i} 
\end{align}</math>

==Steps==
We assume that the matrices are [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] and [[positive-definite matrix|positive definite]], and assume we have scaled the eigenvectors such that

: <math>\mathbf{x}_{0j}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} = \delta_{ij}, \quad 
</math><math>\mathbf{x}_{i}^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{j}= \delta_{ij} \qquad(2)
 
</math>

where {{math|''δ<sub>ij</sub>''}} is the [[Kronecker delta]]. 
Now we want to solve the equation

:<math>\mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}_i - \lambda_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i=0. </math>
In this article we restrict the study to first order perturbation.

===First order expansion of the equation ===
Substituting in (1), we get

:<math>(\mathbf{K}_0+\delta \mathbf{K})(\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta \mathbf{x}_{i}) = \left (\lambda_{0i}+\delta\lambda_{i} \right ) \left (\mathbf{M}_0+ \delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \left (\mathbf{x}_{0i}+\delta\mathbf{x}_{i} \right ),</math>

which expands to

:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} &+ \delta \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{K}_0\delta \mathbf{x}_i + \delta \mathbf{K}\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \\[6pt]
&\lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}+\lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +\delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \\
& \quad \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i.
\end{align}</math>

Canceling from (0) (<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}</math>) leaves

:<math>\begin{align}
\delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + & \mathbf{K}_0\delta \mathbf{x}_i + \delta \mathbf{K}\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \\ & \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i + \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{M}_0\delta\mathbf{x}_i +  \delta\lambda_i \delta \mathbf{M} \delta\mathbf{x}_i.
\end{align}</math>

Removing the higher-order terms, this simplifies to

:<math>\mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad(3)</math>
:In other words, <math>\delta \lambda_i</math>  no longer denotes the exact variation of the eigenvalue but its first order approximation.

As the matrix is symmetric, the unperturbed eigenvectors are <math> M </math> orthogonal and so we use them as a basis for the perturbed eigenvectors. 
That is, we want to construct

:<math>\delta \mathbf{x}_i = \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} \qquad (4) \quad </math> with <math> \varepsilon_{ij}=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T M \delta \mathbf{x}_i </math>,
where the {{math|''ε<sub>ij</sub>''}} are small constants that are to be determined.

In the same way, substituting in (2), and removing higher order terms, we get <math>\delta\mathbf{x}_j \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0j} \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_{i} 
+  \mathbf{x}_{0j} \delta \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}=0 \quad{(5)}</math>

The derivation can go on with two forks.

==== First fork: get first eigenvalue perturbation ====
=====  Eigenvalue perturbation =====
:We start with (3)<math>\quad \mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}; </math>
we left multiply with <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T </math> and use (2) as well as its first order variation (5); we get
:<math> \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i
</math>
or
:<math> \delta \lambda_i=\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} -\lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}
</math>
We notice that it is the first order perturbation of the generalized [[Rayleigh quotient]]  with fixed <math>x_{0i}</math>: <math> R(K,M;x_{0i})=x_{0i}^T K x_{0i}/x_{0i}^TMx_{0i}, \text{ with }x_{0i}^TMx_{0i}=1 </math>

Moreover, for <math>M=I</math>, the formula <math>\delta \lambda_i = x_{0i} ^T \delta K x_{0i}</math> should be compared with [[Bauer–Fike theorem|Bauer-Fike]] theorem which provides a bound for eigenvalue perturbation.

===== Eigenvector perturbation =====
We left multiply (3) with <math> x_{0j}^T </math> for <math> j \neq i </math> and get
:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{K}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} + \delta \lambda_i \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}. </math>
We use <math> \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T K=\lambda_{0j} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^TM \text{ and } \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}=0,
</math> for <math> j \neq i </math>.

:<math>\lambda_{0j} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i} . </math>
or
:<math>(\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i}) \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i+ \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} =  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}  . </math>
As the eigenvalues are assumed to be simple, for <math> j \neq i </math>
:<math> \epsilon_{ij}=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i =\frac{-\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}}{ (\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i})} ,  i=1, \dots N; j=1, \dots N; j \neq i. </math>
Moreover (5) (the first order variation of (2) ) yields
<math> 2 \epsilon_{ii}=2 \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \mathbf{M}_0 \delta x_i=-\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta M \mathbf{x}_{0i} .</math>
We have obtained all the components of <math> \delta x_i </math> .

==== Second fork: Straightforward manipulations ====
Substituting (4) into (3) and rearranging gives
:<math>\begin{align}
\mathbf{K}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} && (5) \\
\sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{K}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} && \\ (\text{applying } \mathbf{K}_0 \text{ to the sum} )\\
\sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \lambda_{0j} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} &= \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \sum_{j=1}^N \varepsilon_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{0j} + \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} && (\text{using Eq. } (1) )
\end{align}</math>

Because the eigenvectors are {{math|'''M'''<sub>0</sub>}}-orthogonal when {{math|'''M'''<sub>0</sub>}} is positive definite, we can remove the summations by left-multiplying by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top</math>:

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \varepsilon_{ii} \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. </math>

By use of equation (1) again:

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{K}_0 \varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\varepsilon_{ii} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}. \qquad (6) </math>

The two terms containing {{math|''ε<sub>ii</sub>''}} are equal because left-multiplying (1) by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top</math> gives

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top\mathbf{K}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i}\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Canceling those terms in (6) leaves

:<math>\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} = \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} + \delta\lambda_i \mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top \mathbf{M}_0\mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Rearranging gives

:<math>\delta\lambda_i  = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K}- \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\mathbf{x}_{0i}^\top\mathbf{M}_0 \mathbf{x}_{0i}}</math>

But by (2), this denominator is equal to 1. Thus

:<math>\delta\lambda_i  = \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

Then, as <math>\lambda_i \neq \lambda_k </math> for <math>i \neq k</math>  (assumption simple eigenvalues) by left-multiplying equation (5) by <math>\mathbf{x}_{0k}^\top</math>:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ik} = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0k} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0k}}, \qquad i\neq k.</math>

Or by changing the name of the indices:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0j} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right )\mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}}, \qquad i\neq j.</math>

To find {{math|''ε<sub>ii</sub>''}}, use the fact that:

:<math>\mathbf{x}^\top_i \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_i = 1</math>

implies:

:<math>\varepsilon_{ii}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i}.</math>

== Summary of the first order perturbation result ==
In the case where '''''all the matrices are Hermitian positive definite and all the eigenvalues are distinct''''', 
:<math>\begin{align}
\lambda_i &= \lambda_{0i} + \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i} \\ 
\mathbf{x}_i &= \mathbf{x}_{0i} \left (1 - \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \mathbf{x}_{0i} \right ) + \sum_{j=1\atop j\neq i}^N \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top_{0j}\left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i}\delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}} \mathbf{x}_{0j}
\end{align}</math>

for infinitesimal <math>\delta\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\delta\mathbf{M}</math> (the higher order terms in (3) being neglected).

So far, we have not proved that these higher order terms may be neglected. This point may be derived using the implicit function theorem; in next section, we summarize the use of this theorem in order to obtain a first order expansion.

== Theoretical derivation ==

=== Perturbation of an implicit function. ===
In the next paragraph, we shall  use the [[Implicit function theorem]] (Statement of the theorem ); we  notice that for a continuously differentiable function <math>f:\R^{n+m} \to \R^m, \; f: (x,y) \mapsto f(x,y)</math>, with an invertible Jacobian matrix  <math> J_{f,b}(x_0,y_0) </math>,  from a point <math> (x_0,y_0) </math> solution of  <math>f(x_0,y_0)=0 </math>, we get solutions of <math>f(x,y)=0 </math> with <math> x</math> close to <math> x_0</math> in the form <math> y=g(x)</math> where <math> g</math> is a continuously differentiable function ; moreover the Jacobian marix of <math> g </math> is provided by the linear system  
 <math> J_{f,y}(x,g(x)) J_{g,x}(x)+J_{f,x}(x,g(x))=0  \quad (6) </math>.
As soon as the hypothesis of the theorem is satisfied, the Jacobian matrix of <math> g </math> may be computed with a first order  expansion of
<math> f(x_0+ \delta x, y_0+\delta y)=0 </math>, we get

<math> J_{f,x}(x,g(x)) \delta x+ J_{f,y}(x,g(x))\delta y=0 </math>; as <math>\delta y=J_{g,x}(x) \delta x </math>, it is equivalent to equation <math> (6) </math>.

=== Eigenvalue perturbation: a theoretical basis. ===
We use the previous paragraph (Perturbation of an implicit function) with somewhat different notations suited to eigenvalue perturbation; we introduce <math> \tilde{f}:  \R^{2n^2}  \times \R^{n+1} \to \R^{n+1}</math>, with
*<math> \tilde{f} (K,M, \lambda,x)= \binom{f(K,M,\lambda,x)}{f_{n+1}(x)}</math> with 
<math>f(K,M, \lambda,x) =Kx -\lambda x, f_{n+1}(M,x)=x^T Mx -1</math>. In order to use the [[Implicit function theorem]], we study the invertibility of the Jacobian <math> J_{\tilde{f};\lambda,x} (K,M;\lambda_{0i},x_{0i})</math> with

<math> J_{\tilde{f};\lambda,x} (K,M;\lambda_i,x_i)(\delta \lambda,\delta x)=\binom{-Mx_i}{0} \delta \lambda  +\binom{K-\lambda M}{2 x_i^T M} \delta x_i</math>. Indeed, the solution of

<math>J_{\tilde{f};\lambda_{0i},x_{0i} } (K,M;\lambda_{0i},x_{0i})(\delta \lambda_i,\delta x_i)=</math><math>\binom{y}{y_{n+1}} </math> may be derived with computations similar to the derivation of the expansion.

<math display="block">  \delta \lambda_i= -x_{0i}^T y, \; \text{ and } (\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j})x_{0j}^T M \delta x_i=x_j^T y, j=1, \dots, n, j \neq i\;;
</math> <math>
 \text{ or }x_{0j}^T M \delta x_i=x_j^T y/(\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}), \text{ and }
\; 2x_{0i}^TM \delta x_i=y_{n+1} </math>

When <math> \lambda_i</math> is a simple eigenvalue, as the eigenvectors <math>x_{0j}, j=1, \dots,n </math> form an orthonormal  basis, for any right-hand side, we have obtained one solution therefore,  the Jacobian is invertible.

The [[Implicit function theorem#Statement of the theorem|implicit function theorem]] provides a continuously differentiable function 
<math> (K,M) \mapsto (\lambda_i(K,M), x_i(K,M))</math>
hence the expansion with [[Big O notation#Little-o notation|little o notation]]:
<math> \lambda_i=\lambda_{0i}+ \delta \lambda_i +o(\| \delta K \|+\|\delta M \|)</math>
<math> x_i=x_{0i}+ \delta x_i +o(\| \delta K \|+\|\delta M \|)</math>.
with

<math> \delta \lambda_i=\mathbf{x}_{0i}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} -\lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0i}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i};</math> <math> \delta x_i=\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_{0j} 
\text{ with}
</math><math>  \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\mathbf{M}_0 \delta\mathbf{x}_i =\frac{-\mathbf{x}_{0j}^T \delta \mathbf{K} \mathbf{x}_{0i} +  \lambda_{0i} \mathbf{x}_{0j}^T\delta \mathbf{M} \mathrm{x}_{0i}}{ (\lambda_{0j}-\lambda_{0i})} ,  i=1, \dots n; j=1, \dots n; j \neq i.</math>
This is the first order expansion of the perturbed eigenvalues and eigenvectors. which is proved.

==Results of sensitivity analysis with respect to the entries of the matrices==
===The results ===
This means it is possible to efficiently do a [[sensitivity analysis]] on {{math|''λ<sub>i</sub>''}} as a function of changes in the entries of the matrices. (Recall that the matrices are symmetric and so changing {{math|'''K'''<sub>''k''ℓ</sub>}} will also change {{math|'''K'''<sub>ℓ''k''</sub>}}, hence the {{math|(2 − ''δ''<sub>''k''ℓ</sub>)}} term.)

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial \lambda_i}{\partial \mathbf{K}_{(k\ell)}} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{K}_{(k\ell)}}\left(\lambda_{0i} + \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i} \right) = x_{0i(k)} x_{0i(\ell)} \left (2 - \delta_{k\ell} \right ) \\
\frac{\partial \lambda_i}{\partial \mathbf{M}_{(k\ell)}} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{M}_{(k\ell)}}\left(\lambda_{0i} + \mathbf{x}^\top_{0i} \left (\delta \mathbf{K} - \lambda_{0i} \delta \mathbf{M} \right ) \mathbf{x}_{0i}\right) = - \lambda_i x_{0i(k)} x_{0i(\ell)} \left (2- \delta_{k\ell} \right ).
\end{align}</math>

Similarly

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_i}{\partial \mathbf{K}_{(k\ell)}} &= \sum_{j=1\atop j\neq i}^N \frac{x_{0j(k)} x_{0i(\ell)} \left (2-\delta_{k\ell} \right )}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}}\mathbf{x}_{0j} \\
\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_i}{\partial \mathbf{M}_{(k\ell)}} &= -\mathbf{x}_{0i}\frac{x_{0i(k)}x_{0i(\ell)}}{2}(2-\delta_{k\ell}) - \sum_{j=1\atop j\neq i}^N \frac{\lambda_{0i}x_{0j(k)} x_{0i(\ell)}}{\lambda_{0i}-\lambda_{0j}}\mathbf{x}_{0j} \left (2-\delta_{k\ell} \right ).
\end{align}</math>

=== Eigenvalue sensitivity, a small example ===
A simple case is <math>K=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & b \\ b & 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>; however you can compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors with the help of online tools such as  [https://wims.univ-cotedazur.fr/wims/wims.cgi] (see introduction in Wikipedia  [[WWW Interactive Multipurpose Server|WIMS]]) or using Sage [[SageMath]]. You get the smallest eigenvalue  <math>\lambda=- \left [\sqrt{ b^2+1} +1 \right]</math> and an explicit computation <math>\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial b}=\frac{-x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}</math>; more over, an associated  eigenvector is <math>\tilde x_0=[x,-(\sqrt{x^2+1}+1))]^T</math>; it is not a unitary vector; so <math>x_{01}x_{02} = \tilde x_{01} \tilde x_{02}/\| \tilde x_0 \|^2</math>; we get <math>\| \tilde x_0 \|^2=2 \sqrt{x^2+1}(\sqrt{x^2+1}+1)</math> and <math>\tilde x_{01} \tilde x_{02} =-x (\sqrt{x^2+1}+1)</math> ; hence <math>x_{01} x_{02}=-\frac{x}{2 \sqrt{x^2+1}}</math>; for  this example, we have checked  that <math>\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial b}= 2x_{01} x_{02}</math> or <math> \delta \lambda=2x_{01} x_{02} \delta b</math>.

== Existence of eigenvectors ==
Note that in the above example we assumed that both the unperturbed and the perturbed systems involved [[symmetric matrices]], which guaranteed the existence of <math>N</math> linearly independent eigenvectors. An eigenvalue problem involving non-symmetric matrices is not guaranteed to have <math>N</math> linearly independent eigenvectors, though a sufficient condition is that <math>\mathbf{K}</math> and <math>\mathbf{M}</math> be [[simultaneously diagonalizable]].

== The case of repeated eigenvalues ==
A technical report of Rellich  <ref>{{Cite book |last=Rellich |first=F. |title=Perturbation theory of eigenvalue problems |year=1954|publisher=CRC Press|
url=https://archive.org/details/perturbationtheo00rell/perturbationtheo00rell}}</ref> for perturbation of eigenvalue problems provides several examples. The elementary examples are in chapter 2. The report may be downloaded from 
[[archive.org]]. We draw an example in which the eigenvectors have a nasty behavior.

=== Example 1 ===
Consider the following matrix <math> B(\epsilon)=  \epsilon \begin{bmatrix}
     \cos(2/\epsilon) &, \sin(2/\epsilon) \\
    \sin(2/\epsilon) &,s   \cos(2/\epsilon) 
\end{bmatrix} </math> 
and <math>A(\epsilon)=I- 
e^{-1/\epsilon^2} B; </math>
<math> A(0)=I. </math>
For <math>\epsilon \neq 0</math>, the matrix <math>A(\epsilon)</math> has eigenvectors <math>\Phi^1=[\cos(1/\epsilon), -\sin(1/\epsilon)]^T; \Phi^2=[\sin(1/\epsilon), -\cos(1/\epsilon)]^T </math> belonging to eigenvalues <math> \lambda_1= 1-e^{-1/\epsilon^2)} , \lambda_2= 1+e^{-1/\epsilon^2)} </math>.
Since <math> \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 </math> for <math> \epsilon \neq 0 </math> if <math>  u^j (\epsilon),
j= 1,2, </math> are any normalized eigenvectors belonging to <math> \lambda_j(\epsilon),j=1,2 </math> respectively
then <math> u^j=e^{\alpha_j(\epsilon)} \Phi^j(\epsilon) </math> where
<math> \alpha_j , j=1,2 </math> are real for <math> \epsilon \neq 0 .</math> 
It is obviously impossible to define <math> \alpha_1(\epsilon) 
</math> , say, in such a way that <math> u^1 (\epsilon) </math> tends to a limit as <math> \epsilon \rightarrow 0 ,</math> because <math> |u^1(\epsilon)|=|\cos(1/\epsilon)|</math> has no limit as <math> \epsilon \rightarrow 0 .</math>

Note in this example that <math> A_{jk} (\epsilon) </math>
is not only continuous but also has continuous derivatives of all orders.
Rellich draws the following important consequence.
<< Since in general the individual eigenvectors do not depend continuously on the perturbation parameter  even though the operator <math>  A(\epsilon) </math> does, it is necessary to work, not  with an eigenvector, but rather with the space spanned by all the eigenvectors belonging to the same eigenvalue. >>

=== Example 2 ===
This example is less nasty that the previous one. Suppose <math>[K_0]</math> is the 2x2 [[identity matrix]], any vector is an eigenvector; then <math>u_0=[1, 1]^T/\sqrt{2}</math> is one possible eigenvector. But if one makes a small perturbation, such as

<math>[K] = [K_0] + \begin{bmatrix}\epsilon & 0 \\0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} </math>

Then the eigenvectors are <math>v_1=[1, 0]^T</math> and <math>v_2=[0, 1]^T</math>; they are constant with respect to <math> \epsilon </math> so that <math> \|u_0-v_1 \| </math> is constant and does not go to zero.
